title: The Lost Tradition of Biblical Debt Cancellations
author: Michael Hudson
desc: La tradición bíblica del jubileo: lo que la Biblia dice sobre la deuda y lo que la iglesia ocultó.
tesis: La Biblia contiene una tradición de cancelación periódica de deudas — el Jubileo del Levítico — que las iglesias cristianas han ignorado sistemáticamente durante dos milenios. 'Perdona nuestras deudas' era literalmente una demanda económica, no una metáfora espiritual. Hudson demuestra que los profetas hebreos eran defensores de los deudores contra los acreedores — una tradición que la iglesia institucional borró para aliarse con los ricos.
ideas: El 'perdón de las deudas' bíblico era literal: cancelación económica, no metáfora espiritual.
La iglesia cristiana ocultó la tradición de cancelación de deudas para aliarse con la clase acreedora.
Los profetas hebreos eran defensores de los deudores — la tradición más radical de la Biblia es económica.
contexto: Publicado en 1993, primer texto de Hudson sobre la tradición bíblica de cancelación de deudas. Su investigación en asiriología con el Harvard Peabody Museum le reveló que el jubileo era práctica económica documentada en tablillas cuneiformes. Este folleto sentó las bases para ...And Forgive Them Their Debts (2018).

conexiones.razon: ...And Forgive desarrolla extensamente lo que Lost Tradition introduce.
Dussel lee las metáforas teológicas de Marx; Hudson lee la economía real de la Biblia.

quotes.text: The new cuneiform discoveries enable us to see how, arising out of a broad Near Eastern matrix, the Biblical laws elevated to the theological plane a by-then revolutionary protest against the arrogance of wealth.

tl: Enmetena de Lagash proclama el primer amar-gi
Enmetena, a ruler of Lagash c. 2404-2375, promulgated the earliest Sumerian debt cancellation on record, c. 2400 BC, after his military victory over the neighboring city of Umma.
Urukagina proclama amar-gi en Lagash

Uruinimgina (2351-42 BC), whose famous 'reform text' inscribed on colored clay cones... 'cleared and cancelled obligations for those indentured families.' ... 'Debt servitude for theft has been abolished.'
Gudea proclama la Pizarra Limpia en Lagash

The longest surviving Sumerian poem (1400 lines) commemorates Gudea's rebuilding of the temple of Gatumdug and the Clean Slate he proclaimed at the New Year festival... 'he remitted debts and granted pardons.'
Reinado de la Tercera Dinastía de Ur

power was seized by UrNammu of Ur (2112-2095). He founded that city's third dynasty... Both father and son seem to have inaugurated their rule with a debt cancellation, as Shulgi pledged to 'establish equity and justice in the land.'
Iddin-Dagan inaugura ciclo de cancelaciones en Isin
During a tumultuous eight decades 1974-1896 BC, five consecutive rulers left inscriptions cancelling debts with nig-sisa acts. The first to do so was Iddin-Dagan (1974-1954).
Lipit-Ishtar libera a hijos de Nippur, Ur e Isin

Lipit-Ishtar (1934-1924 BC), cancelled back taxes and other debts... He 'procured ... the freedom (nig.sisa) of the sons and daughters of Nippur, the sons and daughters of Ur... upon whom slaveship had been imposed.'
Ilushuma proclama andurarum en Ashur

Two Assyrian rulers from 1950-1900 BC - Ilushuma and his successor Erishum - have left building inscriptions commemorating debt cancellations. Ilushuma announces that 'I have established the freedom (andurar) of the Akkadians and their children.'
Sumulael rompe las tablillas en Babilonia

Sumulael (1880-1845), the second ruler of Hammurapi's dynasty, helped prepare the ground for Babylon's expansion by proclaiming freedom from debts at the start of his rule. The word he used, misharum...
Rim-Sin purifica frentes en Larsa

Rim-Sin (1822-1763), proclaimed a Clean Slate, 'purifying the foreheads' of his subjects who had been reduced to debt-servitude... Kraus finds numerous references in Larsa legal contracts to imply that he cancelled debts on at least three occasions.
Hammurabi de Babilonia proclama mīšarum

When Hammurapi succeeded his father in 1792 BC, his inaugural political act likewise was to 'proclaim freedom' with a misharum edict. As in the case of his predecessors, this was considered so important that it was memorialized in his date formula.
Hammurabi promulga edicto de mīšarum en Larsa

He annulled debts again in 1780, 1771 and 1762, and each such occasion seems to have accompanied a conquest... The last one, in 1762 - on the thirtieth 'Jubilee' year of his rule - followed the defeat of Rim-Sin.
Samsuiluna restablece amargi en Sumer y Acad

Hammurapi lay dying in 1749 BC... his son Samsuiluna tells how, upon taking the throne, he found the land so burdened by debt that he remitted the payments... 'The year in which Samsuiluna established freedom (amargi) in Sumer and Akkad.'
Edicto de mīšarum de Ammi-saduqa

Ammisaduqa (1646-1626) took the throne, misharum acts had become very detailed... Ammisaduqa declared misharum upon his accession and again ten years later, in 1636. His act is the longest and most detailed of all the Mesopotamian rulers.
Mursili I saquea Babilonia
No misharum proclamations are found after the rule of Ammisaduqa. In 1595 BC Babylon fell to Iranian mountain tribesmen, the Kassites, who ruled for nearly half a millennium, until 1155 BC.
Nuzi adopta la proclama shudutu hurrita

Nuzi, a Hurrian-speaking town in the land of Arrapha. Its word for debt cancellation was shudutu, a translation of Babylonian simdat, 'proclamation,' connoting a general release or andurarum for real estate as well as for bondservants.
